utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] The affirmation you made still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel. Before we go on, may I ask, Your Honours, in connection with Exhibit D389 which was admitted yesterday, I omitted one fact, namely that it was under seal in the Milutinovic case. Can I now ask you to have that exhibit placed under seal in this instance as well. The number being D389.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, during your testimonies these days as well as in earlier cases, you repeated time and again that you had met with the competent members -- no, that you have acquainted competent members of the General Staff with the disproportionate use of force and that you had impressed that fact many times on General Dimitrijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P1401.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down; the interpreters are unable to catch the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are well prepared, Mr. Djurdjic, with the numbers ready, and you are giving them very quickly. On numbers and dates and names, it pays to be just a little slower. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat, Your Honours, I do apologise. So can we see the Milutinovic case transcript, P1401, page 26627, line -- lines 21 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question -- the transcript starts at 9.700 or so, you did correctly mean 26.627, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, because General Dimitrijevic was the last witness in the Milutinovic case, and he gave his statement on transcript number 26627. That is the transcript number which was in the Milutinovic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript of the testimony of Mr. Dimitrijevic is not an exhibit in this case, and I don't believe it's listed in the list of the exhibits that the Defence intends to use with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have included it. It is on our list, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's always been on the list, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. As the Milosevic case transcript, I'm using Milosevic in cross-examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean Milutinovic? You said Milutinovic earlier, 26.000? You must have meant Milosevic. Milosevic 26.627.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Dimitrijevic was not a witness in the Milosevic case, only in the Milutinovic case. Your Honours, in order not to lose time ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit P1401 may be the transcript that you want. That is the exhibit in this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not going to quote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Crosland, General Dimitrijevic said that you spoke to him about the excessive use of force and that you had a cassette and he asked you to show that cassette, and that you never handed over that cassette to him.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't recall giving a cassette to General Dimitrijevic. I gave a cassette to General Ojdanic via the FLS. And as far as I understand from the Foreign Liaison Service, they maintain they never received it. So where it went to, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in view of the fact that we have all that in the case, the transcript of which is here, I'm not going to dwell on that. I'm just going to say that you never gave any such cassette to General Dimitrijevic, so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not going to help us for you to say it. Are you asking the witness whether he agrees that he didn't give a cassette to General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Your Honour, I didn't give a cassette to General Dimitrijevic. I said there were -- I showed him photographs of the bodies from the Donje Prekaze area which was very early on in 1998, and I told him that these original photographs were now back in various NATO capitals as proof of a massacre that might then be investigated at a later date. I don't know if that helps, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The position you put to the witness, he agrees with, Mr. Djurdjic, so please carry on as you were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, is it the rule when talks are conducted in the General Staff offices with the defence attaches for minutes of meetings where records of those talks to be made as we saw yesterday as the one that we saw yesterday has been made by Jovanovic who was a colonel at that time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I would understand that both sides would make a report. As you know, I have indicated in reports that I had these meetings with General Dimitrijevic, General Perisic, and General Krga, and they are part of the reports that I filed during that period. And I presume the FLS did exactly the same, but I didn't obviously see their reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have D390 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we went through these other items yesterday. What I'm interested in now is that the Colonel Jovanovic notes that is this talk was conducted with you on the 25th of June, 1998, and that you informed him that from the 15th of May to the 25th of June, you had had numerous contacts in Great Britain with military personnel in the armed forces, in the foreign ministry in NATO, with the chief of the military intelligence services, with the chief of operations of the General Staff of Great Britain, the Chief of General Staff, the chief for foreign political affairs in the Ministry of Defence and the commander of the NATO corps for rapid interventions, General Jackson. And that you had informed them about the situation in Kosova-Metohija, and then you also advanced the positions that you advocated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, at that time -- you have three daughters at that time, did the wedding of one of your daughters take place as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wedding of my eldest -- our eldest daughter, rather, took place on the 8th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, 6th of June. I beg your pardon, I shall get slapped by my daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you told us that you had sent a report to the Ministry of Defence on the 28th of May, while at that time you were in Great Britain so that you were in no position to send an [indiscernible] report on the 28th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't understand the question. If you are saying that I couldn't have sent a report, I was still in touch with my -- the person who was standing in for me in Yugoslavia, and if a report was sent via me - because there was going to be a very senior meeting on the 8th of June - that would have been an update to me before this very important meeting on the 8th of June. But as I don't know which report you are referring to, I'm a little bit lost, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, that is Exhibit P1405. Asked by the Prosecutor whether you had participated in the daily tour of western Kosovo, you replied, "yes, I had." That is page 9162, pages 19 to 25. The Prosecutor asked you, and to his question you replied, "There are houses burning in the north of Decani." "Can you tell us exactly what this part referred to, the houses north -- in the north part of Decani?" And you replied saying that you were there personally on the 26th and 27th, whereas on those dates you were in Great Britain, so you were in no position, you were unable to send a report on the 28th of May, whereas you had told us that you -- you told us that you had sent a report on the 28th of May.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, yesterday there were several mistakes in your testimony. Perhaps I shouldn't be saying this, Your Honours, and I respect your charges. If there has been a mistake, then I can assure you it is not my intention to mislead the Court. You were asking me, as I've said many times, to repeat my reports that were made 12 years ago. I think in order to get things moving we need to go either back to the original report, or we are going to go round and round in circles. And it's not my intention to mislead anyone in this report -- or in this court, rather, as I understand the implications that are concerned with it. If there has been a mistake, I apologise, but I cannot recall reports that you keep bringing up without seeing these reports. And I ask that they go back to original report that was tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, the Chamber has not been interfering with your cross-examination, but it was a constant feature yesterday that you would put to the witness a matter from a report without showing the witness the report, and he almost went hoarse saying, well, I can't remember in detail. If it's in my report, it is correct, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, if you feel that there's some error in what he has said or in a report, you need to put that specifically to the witness. And if it is an error in the report, you need to show him the report, so that he can then answer with a clearer memory and recollection than you just ask him about a report on some date in August 1998, and he says, Well, I can't really remember that, but whatever is in there must be right. I hope that will help you to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I believe that I was clear, but I should repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in examination-in-chief you confirm that you personally prepared Exhibit P1405 and that you had toured these parts of Kosova-Metohija. In this report we see that two days were in question. This is one fact. The second fact which I have just now presented to you is that you were absent, that you were outside Yugoslavia from the 25th of June to the 22nd of June, that you were in Great Britain. And I'm telling you that you could not have personally visited these places that are contained in the report of the 28th and that you had not dispatched that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, I think this sort of question is just the point of my comment. You need first to bring up Exhibit P1405, allow the witness to see it. Ask him then whether he made that report. If so, how could he make it if he also said he was in the United Kingdom at that time, and see whether he agrees with you or disagrees with you. We start with Exhibit P1405.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me. I believe I was in England as stated on the -- a current document on the -- well, it's not now, it's gone. It was from the 15th to the 22nd of June. So I don't know quite how the 28th comes into it, by which time I think I was probably back in Belgrade. But I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the document now back again before you. You mention in the second paragraph -- or there it is a document not of you, but of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the FLS, sir, yes, the Foreign Liaison Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Colonel Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. He --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And he notes your absence from the 15th of May to the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That period covered our daughter's wedding, sir. So if it's the 28th of June, I would suspect that I was back in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you referred to Exhibit D390. Now we go to Exhibit P1405, which is your report. And this is the document of -- it seems to be a document dated the 28th of May, not the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes, in which case, I presume I would have written this report, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That was before you went to the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Djurdjic, you followed that. What more is it that you want to ask about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if the witness went to Britain on the 25th and was not here on the 26th and on the 27th, then he could not have sent a report on the 28th of May to the British Ministry of Defence. And apart from that, in examination-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are going in circles, Mr. Djurdjic. Why do you say the witness was in the United Kingdom on those dates in May?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He now confirmed that from the 25th of May to the 22nd of June he had been in Great Britain. From the 25th of May to the 22nd of June the witness was in Great Britain and not in Serbia. This is what the witness has confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, not to my understanding of the evidence. You have asked him orally several times mixing the dates up in almost every question. Now if you want to put to the witness that he was in the United Kingdom, put it specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is it true, and he replied to you, the witness did, is it true that Colonel Jovanovic noted that from the 15th of May to the 22nd of June the witness was in Great Britain. This is what he confirmed to you. Namely, from the 25th of June to the 22nd of June [as interpreted]. Then you present to him the reports of the 28th of May --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You've done it again, Mr. Djurdjic, you've switched months. This is where we are having trouble. It may be a matter of interpretation, it may be that in your excitement to get a point across that you are putting the wrong month. We go back to the proposition that in the Exhibit D390, Colonel Jovanovic noted that the witness was absent from the 25th of May to the 22nd of June. Right. You now want to ask the witness about a report dated the 28th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, not from the 25th of May, from the 15th of May, 1998, to the 22nd of June, 1998, is the time when the witness was in Great Britain. And this is what he has confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we go back, please, to Exhibit D390. Yes, the recording there is the 15th of May to the 22nd of June. Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I help, Your Honours. When I was in England covering my -- our daughter's wedding, there was a delegated stand-in or deputy defence attache which was sworn in and through the FLS to cover my absence. Now, if this is where the supposition is that a report sent by BRITMILREP, that would have been covered by my deputy in my absence in the full knowledge of the FLS. So if that is the -- if that is where the misinterpretation or juxtaposition is, that may be where it's come about. And I know that they were touring in western Kosovo in the Decani area where there was considerable trouble. But if that's where the confusion has happened, Your Honours, then again I apologise, but the FLS would have been informed that a properly recognised deputy was standing in during this absence of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask just a question. Perhaps there is a problem with the interpretation again or translation of this document. Have you been in Great Britain for that time one week or for five weeks, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the date is as on the document now on the screen. I was there for approximately three weeks or four weeks, 15th of May to the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is approximately five weeks. But if you look to the original document in B/C/S, I can't -- think it's quite illegible, but it could be the 16th of June to the 22nd of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite correct, sir. I think that's where the mistake has come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps that is the reason for this misunderstanding. Can we zoom in that perhaps a little bit. The second paragraph of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it says 15/06 to 22/06 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 15th of May. Now it's very clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but it's quite clear that in this document it is written 15th of May until the 22nd of June, and this is exactly how it was translated, so both linguistical versions are quite okay. There is no mistake in translation here, therefore, I would like to point out the following: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Djurdjic, we are going to sort this through. There has been too much confusion about it to leave it as it is. Thank you for that. Could the Court Officer now bring up Exhibit P1405. Mr. Crosland, this is a report which I think you see, appears to be dated the 28th of May, 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And this appears be to a report in the period in which, according to the previous exhibit, you were in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, and it would have been done by my deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So this report here you see from the BRITMILREP, is a report prepared by your deputy rather than yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I would have been in England at that time. Correct, sir. So if that is where the confusion it, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Right. Now, Mr. Djurdjic, you've understood that so far? The witness tells us this report here on the screen was prepared by his deputy, not by him. Now, do you want to question then something about the content of the report or the witness's knowledge of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my initial position was exactly this, and now we've confirmed it was correct. And I asked how come that in direct examination he stated that he personally visited Kosovo on the given two dates, and that he personally wrote this report. This is what he stated when questioned by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The transcript reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reference is 9162, lines 19 to 25. Actually, the pertinent lines are 24 and 25. "Sir, did you participate in the two-day visit to Kosovo on the two given dates?" "A. Yes, I did." So this is page 9162, lines 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you help us there, Mr. Crosland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I've already stated this report - my error - it was done by my deputy. He was travelling with two very experienced other defence attaches, the American and the Canadian. So I would -- the author of the report, forgive me, that is a mistake, I've admitted to that. The actual content, I would suggest, is true because there were two experienced other observers in this particular tour. But I apologise again if I've made a mistake over a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you told us that you were in Kosovo and Metohija between the 12th and 14th of January, 1999. This was on page 9184 of our transcript, lines 16 to 18, and you gave an affirmative answer in lines 19 to 22. And I would like to put to you D005-0321.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could see it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is a transcript in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could kindly see page 8.000. I apologise, 8.005, lines 11 to 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You answered in lines 13 to 15: "I believe I was in Belgrade. I had only just come back from the UK, and I was getting ready to go to Kosovo the following day."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I've already informed the Court, I arrived on the afternoon of Racak, the incident you are talking about presumably. Because of the serious nature, I was asked to go down immediately to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you said that you arrived to Belgrade on the 14th, and here in this -- that's what you stated here in this transcript. And you told us that you were, in fact, in Kosovo and Metohija between the 12th and the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, if we are going to get into a hammering match about dates, then I would ask you, please, to go back to the original documents. Yesterday you produced two undated videos, one showing Ambassador -- the American ambassador - I've forgotten his name - going to Junik, where on that visit he sat with a representative of the Kosovo Liberation Army, which quite naturally upset the Yugoslav representatives. You then switched to Malisevo, and you showed another undated video. Into that film came an old gentleman with a shopkaron [phoen], a classical Albanian hat, outlining the snows of the mountains, a normal Albanian hat. That gentleman lived in the black and white house that was showed on the video where I was personally interrogated twice. I think if there are mistakes in my transcripts, some of it, which the Court has admitted, came about by cutting and pasting, which is a problem with computers. If I've made an error, Your Honours, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, I put to you what you told us during the direct examination by Madam Kravetz, that between the 12th of the 14th of January of 1999 you were touring Kosovo and Metohija. And after that I put on the screen a part of the transcript from the Milosevic case where you stated that on the 14th of January, 1999, you came back from the UK. So it is either or; you could not have been both in the UK and in -- or rather, in Belgrade and in Kosovo and Metohija on the same time. So this is my question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for the promotion to general, but I never made general. I repeat, I arrived, as far as I can remember, in the evening or the late afternoon of the 14th in Kosovo. What are you trying to prove? I beg your pardon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, this means that you weren't touring Kosovo between the 12th and the 14th, as you previously stated because you only arrived to Belgrade from the UK on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, okay, I may have missed the 12th. I seem to recall I went straight, because the seriousness of the situation, down to Kosovo. Yesterday, we had years missing between your dates of various things that happened. We've got one day missing here, so I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, you told us that you came back to Racak on the 16th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the same exhibit, page 7945, lines 20 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You were asked by the Prosecutor: "I would like to go back to the 15th of January, 1999, the incident known as Racak." And then you started your answer. And on page 7949 in lines 6 and 7 when asked whether you were there at the time of the conflict itself, you answered in lines 8 and 9: "I arrived just after the major conflict, but there was considerable activity ongoing that afternoon and throughout that day."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, yes, I've shown there in lines, 12, 13, 14, 15, et cetera, this area around Stimlje, Racak incident area was where the road was blocked by the KLA at a place called Crniljevo. In military terms the Serbs had a very strong force deployed in that area for, I would think months probably. So there was always an interest in that area as to how the situation was progressing. This situation just didn't flare up. As I've told the Court, I think three MUP were killed and the Racak incident took place. But the forces were there in place for quite some time. I think you are trying to make -- as I've said yesterday on many occasions, it was a very fluid situation. And to take a particular incident and try and scrutinize that down, I would suggest, is not the way to get to the bottom of the problem. And I'm not quite certain which way you are going, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on the 15th of January, 1999, were you present in Racak during the combat activities when the artillery guns were fired?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness has already answered this question. It has been put to him in different ways. He has already indicated when he arrived back in Kosovo, and indicated that was after the incident. It's been covered in cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it may be clear to you; it's not quite yet clear to me, Ms. Kravetz. I think Mr. Djurdjic should continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So as far as I can remember, the incident happened and was over by the 14th. Quite rightly the Yugoslav authorities were not allowing people into the area because it was not declared a safe area. So there was an ongoing military incident in that area, which was observable, and quite rightly, they weren't allowing us any closer other than the OSCE/Kosovo Verification Mission, KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, the core issue here is that in these quotations that I'm putting to you now, and I have more of them, you did state that on the 15th of May you were in the immediate vicinity of Racak during the time of conflict. So is that right what is written in these transcripts? And as I said I have more of these if you want me to show them to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I've just told you that an ongoing military incident is not an area that you allow outsiders into for very obvious reasons. Now, "within the immediate vicinity of the area" could be within a couple of kilometres, et cetera. So, yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The witness has already responded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask something very direct. Are you able to recall now whether you were in Racak on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in Racak is not possible because it's a village off the main road. So in the area or the vicinity of Racak, I would suggest, is a more general term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point is, were you there in your recollection on the 15th, or was it on the 16th that you arrived, or is it unclear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest, it is unclear, sir. But if you say "in Racak," that is not accurate. It is in the vicinity of Racak. A military incident covers a big area, and as I've said before quite obviously, they would not allow other people into the area until they declared it safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask the Exhibit D005-0649, paragraph 15. This is page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is your statement from December 1992, Colonel. Which says the following: "In Racak there was also KLA with a small headquarters. In the attack on 15th of January, 1999, which I witnessed from my arrival sometime in the afternoon to about 1400 hours involved element of Colonel Jelic's 243rd Mechanised Brigade and included BOV-3s, T-55 mortars, and D-30 Howitzers."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I have written that report, then that is a correct example. But as I say, I would suggest you are saying "in Racak." It's not possible to be in Racak. It's in the vicinity of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I accept that. But the point is that you claim both in the Milosevic case and here in this statement that you were present and that you observed from that place where you were on the 15th, that you observed the fighting. You even described some details here. Whereas to us here, you said that you arrived to Racak on the 16th, after the incident had already taken place.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are now getting back to dates again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Not, sir. It is one thing to be present during the event and witness it, and it is another thing to arrive afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, I have just tried to explain you cannot witness an action going on when there is heavy firing going on, because the military, quite rightly, do not want outsiders looking over their shoulders. You can be in the area which could be as far away as 10 kilometres away when heavy gun-fire would be falling in areas, and you can observe the gun-fire from a considerable distance as has been proven with Lord Ashdown in the Suva Reka area. Now, you are not physically in the vicinity. You are quite some way away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to see once again D005-0321, page 8.005, lines 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, when asked: "Given the events in Racak given that you were there on January the 15th, did you report on that?" You answer in line 18: "I sent -- there is a written report, as I think had been explained to you, and I used to be in communication by other means back to both Belgrade and to the United Kingdom."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that is exactly correct. Some reports I sent by secure communication direct to the Ministry of Defence, particularly if they were of such a serious nature as was currently going on in the Racak area. There may well not have been a written report, because there was not time to write a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, but you told us here during the direct examination that you only came to Racak after the event on the 16th and 17th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are back to dates again, Your Honour. And if there's been confusion, there's been confusion. What was quite obvious, was that there had been a very serious incident in the Racak area which was covered by OSCE and KVM. If I came a day later, then I apologise. What are you inferring, my integrity? I want an answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will do. That will do, Mr. Djurdjic. Mr. Crosland, the evidence that you have given leaves me quite unclear about two subject matters relating to Racak. The first is this: Do you have a clear recollection of when you arrived and how long you were there? If so, what is that recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I don't have a clear recollection, no. Twelve years ago, and I am afraid things have moved on. But my initial reports, I believe, are the true reports. I've been questioned, as you know, Your Honour, many times by this court. I've seen many reports be cut and pasted and mistakes have been made. And as we saw yesterday, Mr. Djurdjic had the same problem. Now, if that has happened, I'm sorry, but I can't be held responsible for that. If there is an error of a day or two days, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The content of the written reports appear to have been made by you relating to the Racak incident; are those contents, contents that you vouch for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd have to recheck. I think I've been asked about Racak on several occasions. I would have to recheck that. Under oath I can't tell you definitely which way, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Were you there in the area of Racak at any time when the conflict was actually occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've said that the conflict -- the incident at Racak was over by the time I got there. I arrived for the aftermath of that particular incident. And the forces concerned were then still deployed in and around the Racak area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You reported on those forces as you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reported on those forces as I'd seen them, and as I stated to Your Honours, these forces had been in position for quite sometime, and occasionally I used to go through their -- or many times I used to go through their check-points on further into the KLA area as part of my normal touring in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, at the beginning of your direct examination when asked by my learned friend, Madam Kravetz, you said that you stand fully behind your statement given on 31st of October, 2006, and the transcript from the Milutinovic case. In that statement, and also in your answers to questions asked by Madam Kravetz, you stated that you came to Racak on the 16th and 17th of January, 1999. In the evidence I put to you from the Milosevic case and in your statement that you gave in the year 2000, you stated that you were present during the conflict in Racak on January the 15th, and this final report that you just talked about was not included into evidence by the Prosecution, and the Defence doesn't have it. All we know is that you stated that you were present in Racak on the 15th during the fighting. So the things are very clear. You could not have been in Racak on the 15th during the event if you came there on the 16th and the 17th. So your statements in two cases are entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has just clarified this matter when responding to questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Djurdjic. It may have been dealt with sufficiently, but is there any further comment, Mr. Crosland, you want to put to what has just been put to you by Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think there may have been a mistake in translation or interpretation, for which again I apologise. This incident, as I've attempted to explain, the nature of the incident, I would suggest, is slightly more serious than actually questioning which date is the actual date. I've said that I arrived after the incident had happened. I have detailed knowledge that I've indicated to you about which units were involved in that particular incident because of my more or less daily touring in the area. Now, I apologise if I've made a mistake on that to the Court. But what I've said I would hope is accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I accept your explanation, but you also gave an oath in the Milutinovic case when you gave a different statement, so this is why I put this to you. And you also gave such a statement in the year 2000 because it is very relevant whether you directly witnessed the incident or not. I apologise for your answers [as interpreted] if they in any way were hurtful to you. This was certainly not my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you, I have no further questions for Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Kravetz, would you think it convenient to have a break now before you re-examine, or would you wish to go straight into re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have very few questions. I think I can finish before the break. I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We were giving you an opportunity to collect your notes or your thoughts, but we are happier to carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to have a break if that's what the Court wishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to direct your attention first to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: If we could have that up on the screen. It's 65 ter 02645. I don't know if you have it before you still or not. I would like for page 8 to be displayed, and it's page 10 in the B/C/S. Specifically I'm looking for paragraph 35. I think that's there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about your whereabouts in the period of May or June 1998, And I think that specific issue has been clarified. But I just wanted to direct your attention to this paragraph which refers to one of the sitreps that was shown to you which the Defence. And it is referred in the statement as Exhibit 00687, and in these proceeds it's Exhibit P10 -- 405. I just wanted to ask you a question. In your statement you indicate that that sitrep and the next one of 5th of June was produced -- were produced by Nick Slinger. Could you explain to the Court who he was.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my authorised deputy during my absence in the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: So that's the person you spoke about earlier during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, ma'am, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And in your statement you say that to your position of DA, you can sponsor the contents of this report. And do you still stand by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained to the Court, Colonel Slinger, was in the company of both an American -- senior American and a senior Canadian defence attache.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Now if we could have Exhibit D331 up on the screen: And I would like page 2 to be displayed for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: This is a daily combat report that you were shown of the 3rd Army to the General Staff of the VJ that you were shown yesterday during cross-examination by my learned colleague from the Defence. And my learned colleague referred you to item 3 which is an item called -- entitled "Situation in Army Units" and referred you to the sentence that says, It is stated that army units, [indiscernible] units in accordance with a decision on engagement. And you agreed that that's what the report stated. And then you made the comment, I just draw the Court's attention to the amount of ammunition fired. And -- which is -- we see displayed in -- on the screen at the bottom of this page. And I just wanted to ask you about that comment, if you could elaborate why you wish to draw the Court's attention to the amount of ammunition fired according to this report.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular instance the amount of ammunition fired, just indicates, as I've said all along, the amount of wanton damage that was done throughout Kosovo, most of it due to firing from the Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic. Sorry, I thought you had finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I should have indicated, Your Honours, that this answer was given at transcript page 9243.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've interrupted the witness. Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this answer has been completed, and I believe it has, I object because this is an opinion that has been uttered here, and the witness was not present and he could not have been aware about the nature of the operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the factual foundation for his evidence is sufficient, Mr. Djurdjic. Carry on, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And just to follow up on the answer that you just gave since we have -- we did interrupt you, you say in this particular incidence the amount of ammunition fired just indicates what you said all along, the amount of wanton damage. Why specifically when you saw this report that came to mind? I mean, what was specific information in this report that made you want to draw the Court's attention to this issue?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way along, the questioning has been doubting the amount of damage that was done throughout Kosova-Metohija during the 1998 to 1999. I don't understand why the Defence doesn't either understand that or accept it. But I, as I've stated, I saw a huge number of villages that were destroyed, and this was viewed by both the Trojka group, the G8, Lord Ashdown, and many other international agencies. And as I've said, if you go and destroy the houses of he local population --

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Sir, if I may interrupt you there, I'm just asking specifically about this report. If there was something specific about this report that made you want to draw the Court's attention to the amount of ammunition fired that's indicated there.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are looking at specific calibres, then the 20-millimetre, the 30-millimetre rounds are anti-aircraft shells, which as I said, were used to flatten houses which is not really a peacekeeping type of weapon. That's just a personal comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one final point, you have been asked several questions about the Racak incident, and if you were there when it occurred and the dates that you arrived back to Kosovo in January. In response to a question of Judge Parker today, and this is at page 21 of the transcript, you were asked if you were there in the area of Racak at any time when the conflict was actually occurring, and you said: "No. The incident of Racak was over by the time I got there. I arrived for the aftermath of that particular incident." Do you recall or have any information as to when - and I'm referring at what time of the day - or the actual incident or the attack on the village of Racak took place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I wasn't present when the attack took place. So I can't help you on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kravetz. Well, you'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questions for you, Mr. Crosland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to thank you for your further attendance here, and the assistance that you've been able to give us over now two and a half days. We are sorry that you have delayed -- been delayed longer than you had anticipated, but it has been necessary to conclude your evidence satisfactorily. We thank you, you may of course now return to your normal activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: The witness may be excused. Yes, it's not related to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have a very small matter to raise, that I wish to deal with before we break. And this concerns an oral application to change the status of portions of the transcript of the testimony of a previous witness, Mr. Phillips, from confidential to public, and also change the status of an exhibit that was tendered through this witness from under seal to public. Since this witness gave evidence, the Rule 70 provider has reviewed the transcript of this testimony. And portions of the testimony were given in private session in order to protect the confidentiality of certain documents that had been provided to the Office of the Prosecution under Rule 70. Having reviewed the transcript, the Rule 70 provider is now happy to release these portions of the transcript to the public, and I can indicate the transcript pages which are concerned, just for reference. And these are transcript pages 8713 to 8737, 8790 to 8793, 8799 to 8823, and 8831 to 8840. So these are the pages of the transcript which were in private session, and we would ask for those to be released to the public. There's also one exhibit. This is Exhibit P1312 which was admitted under seal and again the Rule 70 provider has authorised us to make that a public exhibit. So we would ask -- it's a double motion for those two issues to be granted by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any observation, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in order to waste too much time here today, I would kindly ask for you to allow us some time to consider this. I'm rather surprised with this move by the Prosecution. I would have expected them to consider this issue before the witness came to testify, so to consider the possibility to remove the confidentiality. But now it seems that after the testimony was given, they have thought about the possibility to remove the confidentiality from the testimony and this also includes some exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can briefly address that. The issue of the confidentiality of this portions of the transcript is not a matter that -- for us to deal with. It's for the Rule 70 provider to authorise and the -- obviously we can only send the complete transcript of the testimony to the Rule 70 provider once the witness has completed his testimony, and we proceeded in this same fashion with the transcript of the testimony of the other Rule 70 witness, Mr. Shaun Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Djurdjic, what it is that you think you would need to reflect upon? It's evidence that has been given. There's a transcript of it. And there's one exhibit. The witness, because of the position taken by the provider, was received in private session and treated as confidential. That was solely because of the position of the provider. The provider now says, well, we've looked at what has been said, and we are content for it now to be a matter of public knowledge. It's not clear to me what it is that -- how it would adversely affect you if it became public.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm quite clear on the matter, and I agree. I wasn't clear before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The confidential recording of part of the evidence of the witness Michael Phillips, as identified in the submission of Ms. Kravetz, will now be made public and similarly the exhibit to which she specifically referred.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, I do want to clarify one point. In portions of those transcript pages, there are also exhibits that the Defence used and which were tendered under seal. We are not authorised, as they are not our exhibits, to request that the seal be lifted, so should the Defence wish to make those exhibits public exhibits, they would need to file their own or -- send their own request to the Rule 70 provider with regard to that. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not affected by your motion. Your motion is only the oral evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: That is true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And one exhibit which you've identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Which is our exhibit, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We've made our order in respect of those matters only. Thank you. Now, we wish to hear the submissions of counsel in respect of the proposal concerning witness K87, and for that purpose we will adjourn now to resume at 10 minutes past 4.00 with a view to hearing those submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we hear submissions under Rule 98 bis, the Chamber would like to deal with one matter, which is the Prosecution's third motion to amend the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. This arose at the time of the evidence given by Aleksandar Vasiljevic in June. It was proposed to add 17 documents to the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter list. That was opposed by the Defence in submissions given on the 8th of June. The Chamber, by oral decision on the 8th of June, allowed the documents to be put to the witness Vasiljevic, and those documents were marked for identification pending this decision and a decision on a motion made in the course of the hearing then for the admission of each of those documents into evidence. Vasiljevic was specifically questioned by the Prosecution only in respect of two of the 17 documents, and there was no cross-examination on any of them. There is no specific justification given for the Prosecution's delay in seeking to add the documents to its exhibit list in the circumstances that have been mentioned, but each of the documents were documents that had been referred to or relied upon by Mr. Vasiljevic in the preparation of his evidence. The Chamber is of the view that the late addition of these documents to the Rule 65 ter list would not, in the circumstances that we've described, prejudice the rights of the accused. I've mentioned that during the evidence, the Prosecution also sought then to tender each of the 17 documents as exhibits. The documents themselves relate to deployment of MUP and VJ forces in Kosovo at times relevant to the indictment. The documents were issued by official sources, as indicated either by official stamps or seals or the signatures of persons holding positions of authority. In those circumstances, the documents are considered to have a sufficient probative value for the purposes of accepting their admission into evidence. The Chamber is able to reach that conclusion essentially on the basis of the 17 documents themselves as it is not -- it is not the case that there has been any detailed discussion of the documents, their contents, or their reliability in the evidence of the witness Vasiljevic or any other witness. Having regard to those matters, the Chamber is persuaded in the end that it would be in the interest of justice, first, to allow the 17 documents to be added to the Prosecution's Rule 65 list, they are set out in Appendix A of the corrigendum to that list. And the Chamber is further of the view that each of those documents should be admitted into evidence. They will be the orders of the Chamber. We now come to the question of Rule 92 quater, and the evidence that is proposed to be tendered of the witness known in these proceedings as K87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The documents I've mentioned in the respect of the previous motion will be admitted as public exhibits. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good afternoon. The motion was filed confidentially and the issue was just raised to me as to whether or not this hearing should be confidential. Actually, I'm not sure that it needs to be if we express ourselves in a manner that does not reveal any confidential information. But I'm in the hands of the Court in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not inclined at the moment to see reason for continued confidentiality. The normal practice is to file matters confidentially where there is likely to be personal information, including information as to health of a person, including a witness, but it would seem at the moment that that is not really a critical issue on this present application.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. I'll proceed, and if myself and I'm sure counsel on the other side think that we need to go into private session, we'll make the appropriate application. Your Honours, if it pleases you, the Prosecution refers to the motion filed on the 22nd of October, that the statement and transcript of K87 be received under Rule 92 quater. And for the purpose of these arguments, I adopt the submissions made in the written file. There is not much that I have to add to it. The matter is squarely before Your Honours as a matter to exercise your discretion as to whether or not you should have available to you at the end of the case the documents in question. The issue is admissibility at this stage, not weight. Indeed, most of the arguments that I could think of to add were arguments that would bolster the weight of these statements, arguments I think the Prosecution can and will legitimately make. But I don't think that this would be the appropriate time to make the arguments about weight. If I may, however, Your Honours, just make one or two additions. In paragraph 15 of the motion, the Prosecution submits that the evidence of K87 is corroborated to the extent that it fits within a larger framework of evidence in the case. And that larger framework of evidence in the case is evidence of the accused's participation in the concealment of the bodies in Serbia. I would respectfully ask Your Honours to refer to the statements of -- or the evidence before the Court of former SUP chiefs Keric and Golubovic who testified about orders they also received from the accused in respect to the burial of the bodies. In respect to -- I also refer the Court to the evidence of K88 that is discussed at paragraph 11 of the motion. K84, also K84 is a witness who led the initial Working Group investigation of the matter. He took K87's original statement and took statements from other persons including drivers, which these statements form a broad framework of evidence which is substantially corroborate K87 in what he has said was his participation and the participation of the accused. And also, Your Honour, I'd ask Your Honour to refer to the evidence of K93, one of the drivers who -- whose evidence was to the effect that he transported bodies from Serbia and also bodies from one truck that had been left in the Danube river, and that he transferred those bodies to Batajnica. And that also when the issue arose, when the -- the concealment of the bodies was revealed in the press, he -- the accused was present with General Lukic when his transfer to another part of Serbia take him out of the limelight was discussed. So those are just four or five witnesses. And as far as K84 is concerned, the documents that accompany his testimony that form part of the broad framework we refer to in paragraph 15, that is substantially on all fours with the evidence that we propose to receive by the Court. Secondly, Your Honours, if I may seek to augment the arguments that we made in paragraph 16 of the motion. This is paragraph discussing the submissions as to why Your Honours should admit the statements, not withstanding that it refers to the acts and conduct of the accused. There have been quite a few cases in this Tribunal where statements referring to the acts and conducts of the accused have been received under 92 quater. And I think I should, for the record, just cite two of them. And that is the Prosecutor against Popovic et al., the decision on the Prosecution motion for a motion of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 quater of the 21st of April, 2008. And also the Prosecutor against Milutinovic et al., the decision on the Prosecution motion for admission of evidence pursuant to Rule 92 quater of the 5th of March, 2007 in -- particularly in paragraph 9 in the Milutinovic decision and paragraph 35, and thereafter in the Popovic decision. Those are cases, Your Honours, among others where statements going to the acts and conduct of the accused were admitted. And these decisions emphasise a point that it is just a factor, one factor, for the Court to consider in exercising its discretion. And it's a factor really counselling cautious scrutiny of the evidence. The circumstances in which it was taken and the extent to which it is corroborated, in particular. But all of these cases, indeed the rule itself, contemplates that these statements are admissible in appropriate circumstances, which we submit is the situation in this case. And thirdly and last, Your Honour, if I may perhaps redundantly, but I will nonetheless briefly just mention and remind the Court that the -- there is a next decision, another decision in the Milutinovic case in respect to 92 quater, that is cited in footnote 2 of the present motion, the instant motion before the Court. And that is the decision of the 16th of February, 2007, and I just refer to paragraph 9 of that decision where it's also discussed that even if there is lack of cross-examination, the statements can be admissible if they -- other circumstances -- all the circumstances considered together make it appropriate to do so. So the absence of cross-examination does not automatically preclude admission of the evidence. In this case the statement -- there was no cross-examination in the making of the statement, but there were opportunities by four or five counsel to cross-examine in the Milutinovic case, and indeed in this case the evidence of Mr. Trajkovic which substantially corroborates what K87 said was also open to cross-examination by counsel in this case. That, Your Honours, for the present is all I have to add to the written submissions. May it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. First of all, I would like to emphasise the chronology of events relating to the testimony of witness K87. Based on the Prosecution reports that we have received, one can deduce that on the 1st and the 21st of August of this year, the Prosecution was again in contact with the witness. I don't want to go any further back into the history because it's irrelevant. At that time the said witness informed the Prosecution about the fact that it is necessary -- I have to stop for a moment because Ms. O'Leary has just pointed out to me that I should ask you whether we should go into private session for them, although I'm not going to mention any names. In my view it's not unnecessary, but I would be grateful for your guidance, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have seen no reason for that, but if there's something that concerns you, please mention it because we don't want to create a problem by oversight. But this was mentioned briefly by Mr. Stamp, we couldn't see any reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On the 21st of August, the witness informed the OTP that he had a medical check-up scheduled for the 29th of August. I have here a Prosecution notice to the effect that the Defence was advised on the 29th that -- on the 29th of September that on the 5th October, the witness will be available for hearing. At that time they already knew that he was going to see the doctor. After that, the Prosecution got in touch with the witness on the 30th of September, and on that day, the witness informed them that he was due to undergo an operation on the 6th of October, 2009. At the Prosecution's request, the witness provided medical records, i.e., referral for a day hospital, and then ergometry department report, dated the 29th of September. Based on these records and documents, the Prosecution investigator concluded that there were no -- there was no evidence that there was any surgery scheduled on the 6th of October, 2009, and that, therefore, a witness wouldn't be able to testify. Let us just look at this order of events that we have been informed about by the Prosecution. It's evident that the Prosecution knew that on the 6th of October, 2009, the witness would not be available. If he had a referral for day hospital dated the 1st of October, that means, that she will have to stay in a medical institution. Later we are going to see that immediately after this information was revealed, the OTP contacted the medical institution where this witness was hospitalised. I think that their best intention was to expedite the proceedings, but the OTP submitted documents to this Trial Chamber, and bearing in mind everything that I said earlier, failed to provide a report dated the 7th of October, 2009, received from the physician who works at the hospital where the witness was hospitalised. In other words, these documents were not submitted to the Trial Chamber before the Chamber decided to schedule the videolink testimony for the 16th. Although the OTP had some prior information, but they deprived the Trial Chamber of that information. What I want to say is, that the Prosecution disclosed all this information to the Defence on the 13th of October. Let us just look what is said in these medical reports. They only show that the witness is only temporarily incapacitated, and it has been very specifically described. In one report it is said that he is not able to go to work for three weeks, and in response to the request by the Prosecution received on the 7th of October, it is said that the patient would be re-examined one month later to see what his condition is. I think that based on these indications, we have no proof that this witness is permanently unavailable. In other words, that his health, both physical and mental, is such that he is permanently unable to testify. Your Honours, based on these medical reports we see that this witness is unable to work only for a period of 30 days following the surgery, which took place on the 5th of October. So this 30-day period will expire in about five or six days. Therefore, we believe that there is no evidence that his health condition is such that at this point due to psychological and physical ailments, this witness is incapable of testifying. And what the Prosecution has rightly and fairly pointed out, at no point was it said in these reports that he was incapable of testifying. However, this incapability is limited to a 30-day period during which period he should be spared any work in any other efforts. After the expiry of this period, he will probably be able to work and anyone who is capable of working, I think, is capable of testifying. But I think that that should be left to the medical expert to decide. Therefore, in my view, this submission that there is permanent incapacity on the part of the witness cannot be acceptable. Since we have written records, we can see that there are definitely all requirements met for a videolink testimony. However, these risks will be eliminated in a matter of course of three or four weeks when the witness becomes healthy again, and I don't see any reason for him not to testify. I would like to address Rule 92 quater now. Pursuant to this rule and concerning this other alternative which says that a person that is incapable of testifying viva voce due to bodily or mental condition, as far as this particular witness is concerned, will be able to testify in about seven or eight days' time. What I would like to underline here is the following: Mr. -- [overlapping speakers]... statement said that this witness was not cross-examined in Milutinovic. That is true, there was no interest on the part of the Defence to cross-examine this witness. And I think this is a crucial point and that the Trial Chamber should particularly take this into account when delivering their ruling. I would also like to point to another fact. We are dealing here with a witness who is to testify about the acts and conduct of the accused for which he is charged in the indictment. If the Prosecution believes that this testimony is unnecessary, they could have relinquished it. But, however, it seems that they believe this testimony is going to be relevant, particularly for the portions of the indictment containing the charges against the accused. Why cross-examination is required? Precisely because, as Mr. Stamp put it today, K87 had given statement and it is already part of this proceedings and which has been admitted into evidence. When this witness testified in Milutinovic, during the briefing with the Prosecution, he denied the statement he gave to this witness. He qualified that as an informal conversation that the content of this conversation was misinterpreted and misrepresented, that he wished to withdraw it. The Defence was notified of this and, therefore, did not conduct cross-examination. Now the Prosecution is arguing that the cross-examination is not necessary in this case either. I think that this witness should and must be cross-examined. And one more thing, although the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you be a little more specific. Are you saying that the witness K87 said that the statement given was a misinterpreted and misrepresented statement, or is it another witness speaking about the conversation with K87?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was probably not accurate enough. When K87 came to testify in Milutinovic, he had a proofing session with the Prosecution beforehand. The Prosecution informed the Defence that the witness told the Prosecution that the statement that he had -- that K84 gave a statement which was misinterpreted, that the contents were wrong, and that this was actually not his statement. K84 is also present in this trial and in this case. Through K84, this statement has been admitted into evidence in this case, the statement claimed by K87 not to have been given by K84. And it's, nevertheless, became part of the evidence. Since the Prosecutor in the Milutinovic case did not wish to rectify this in examination-in-chief, and to put to the witness, and there was no subsequent cross-examination, the matter was left as it was. We only have a notification by the Prosecution in the Milutinovic case that the witness denied having given a statement to our witness K84. I believe that this is proper grounds for cross-examining witness K87 because that is one of the crucial and fundamental reason for doing so. I don't know if I was clear enough on this matter. Or maybe I should try to clarify it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are slow this afternoon, Mr. Djurdjic, I'm sure. It is not clear to me, are you saying that K87 has said that his evidence concerning your client of conversations between K87 and your client is not correct, has been misinterpreted or misrepresented? Or are you talking about some other event that concerns witness K84?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in our proceedings we heard witness K84, who was in charge of MUP group and took statements from different witnesses, and those statements were as such tendered into evidence through K84. In the Milutinovic case, witness K87 came and told the Prosecutor that statement taken by the Working Group, i.e., by witness K84, that witness is not correct. Am I clear, and have I managed to explain now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The point is that at the hearing, the Prosecutor also failed to avail himself of the possibility of telling the witness, excuse me, just as what the K84 has drawn up does not correspond to the truth. The Defence did not cross-examine him, and it remained as such. Now we have that statement in the case file via witness K84. May I also say this, I believe that by adoption of these documents of the transcript and these statements according to Rule 92 quater without cross-examination, we would infringe upon the accused's right to a Defence. There is another thing which is untrue which we heard here, which is that protected witness K93 had said that Mr. Lukic had participated with the accused in the transportation of bodies. Mr. K93 had never said any such thing here, and this is something that you can verify for yourselves by reading our transcripts. Bearing in mind this state of facts, I'm referring to the health condition of the person referred to, this witness, namely when we -- seem that we waited for four or five weeks for Mr. Crosland, perhaps this Chamber could or should also wait for another ten days until we get a medical report to the effect whether this witness is indeed capable of taking the stand or not. I think it would be a minimal loss and practically no damage done, no harm done relevant to the potential damage that could be done to the accused and to his right to a Defence if we were to rule today on the basis of -- to make a decision today on the basis of Rule 92 quater. I, therefore, move that the Chamber do not rule instantaneously, but for us to wait for the relevant medical reports, and only then on their basis bring just decision. This is what I wanted to point out because in the course of proceedings so far, I believe that the proceedings have been conducted to the satisfaction of all parties in the proceedings, and that at this juncture we are for the first time at a juncture where potentially harmful or perhaps erroneous decision might be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that we are clear, you are directly urging that we should delay the progress of the trial to receive a further medical report when it becomes available?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honours, on the basis of the existent document, the Defence deems that it has not been ascertained that this witness is permanently incapacitated physically and mentally to take the witness-stand and that the relevant records and data will be available to the Trial Chamber only in a matter of seven days, after his scheduled check-up, and that it should only then rule. The Defence does accept that if the medical record were to show that he is not capable of taking the witness-stand on medical grounds, then of course the Trial Chamber would have grounds to decide whether requirements under 92 quater have been met or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I notice that you have several times spoken of it not being established that the witness is permanently unable to testify. I don't see the word permanently in Rule 92 quater A. Merely that he is or she is unable to testify orally. Now this of course is a separate issue from whether it may be the case that the witness will be fit to give evidence in a week or two's time, as you suggest. But do you accept that there's no specific requirement that the witness be permanently unable to testify from the rule?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now this is within the realm of interpretation. I believe that in a ruling of yours referring to a witness which had been accepted under 92 quater on these grounds, mentally and physically unable, namely that you adopted the position that that was a chronic condition with him, referring to his health of course. Now we are speaking about such a health problem in view of the progress of medical equipment, that this is a routine operation, routine surgery. It is just -- and recuperation will take only a short time. It is just as if somebody would have not been able to come on account of a simple flu. So that within a matter of days that person would have recovered. It is true that this is -- the word permanent is not contained in the article. But it does say that the bodily and mental or physical incapacitation is of a lengthier duration on account of which he will not be available to court. Now, had he been cross-examined in the Milutinovic case, it would be easier to take a decision. Now we have two elements here. A, there was no cross-examination; and secondly, his questionable health condition. If he recuperates within a couple of days, and it is a short period, I believe that we should wait because we waited for Crosland for such a long time. And I believe that it is of the essence in this particular case. And another thing, which I wish to underline, after the cross-examination you have to assess the evidence presented, of course. If this is such an important witness for the Prosecution, I believe that it is only fair and correct for the Defence to cross-examine that witness. And this is yet another argument in favour of the statements that have already been admitted, and we have, of course, the written statement of the OTP that he had recanted his words, but that will not be tendered as evidence unless we cross-examine this witness. If I put myself in the shoes of the judge, despite the fact that it is not expressly stated in this article that it should not be a permanent condition, account should be taken of the nature of the incapacity, the physical and mental incapacity of the witness, which is in question for the Trial Chamber to rule. Of course, something can be acute and short-lived, and other conditions can be permanent or chronic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You did mention a previous decision in which I had been a judge. Do you have a reference to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have one, Your Honours, but now with the papers that I have in front of me, of which there are many -- let me just try and find my bearings. Well, IT-05-87/1-T of the 19th of August, 2009. It is witness Zhuniqi, Ms. O'Leary just reminded me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is a decision in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your decision, your Chamber, your case, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it reciting merely that in that case there was a chronic condition, or is it your submission that it was said to be a requirement that there be a chronic condition?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I shall read it out for you. You noted that in the documents it was stated the use of Zhuniqi had had a brain stroke, was unable to speak, and was not emotionally stable enough to be able to testify. So on the basis of all those documents, you concluded that he was unavailable. "According to the opinion of the Chamber, these documents clearly attest to the physical and mental condition of the witness and to the fact that he is unable to testify."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Firstly, if I might deal with the last thing. The passage referred to in the decision with respect to Zhuniqi is at paragraph 8.
